title: The burden rolls away
hook: in Bunyan's story, Christian's burden falls off at the cross and rolls into a tomb

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bunyan in jail, and Evangelist pointing the way. Your line was the dream in the jail.

A heavy backpack does something strange on a long hike. At first you feel every pound. Then you stop noticing, you lean forward without knowing it, and your shoulders forget what light felt like. Only when you set it down do you realize how bent you'd become. Bunyan's pilgrim starts like that. The first picture of him is a man in rags with a great burden on his back, reading a book and crying out, What shall I do? He carries that weight through the slough, past the gate, mile after mile. Today, in the story, it finally comes off.

Christian runs, with difficulty, up a road fenced with a wall on either side, to a place that rises a little. At the top stands a cross, and below it, a tomb. Here's how Bunyan tells it: "Just as Christian came up with the Cross, his burden loosed from off his shoulders, and fell from off his back, and began to tumble, and so continued to do, till it came to the mouth of the Sepulchre, where it fell in, and I saw it no more." Look at what Christian does in that sentence. Nothing. He doesn't untie the straps or throw it off. He arrives, and the burden loosens. Bunyan, a Protestant preacher, is picturing what he believed about grace: that what Christ did on the cross lifts a weight a person can't lift alone. The burden falls into the sepulchre, which some readers take as Christ's own tomb, and the narrator never sees it again. Christian stands looking at the cross, amazed, tears running down his cheeks. Then he says, "He hath given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death." Rest. That reaches back to Jesus in Matthew's gospel: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Christians from different churches describe how that rest comes in different ways: through baptism and the sacraments, through faith, through confession, through a lifetime of being made new. Bunyan's picture is one man's dream of it. And the road doesn't end at the cross. Christian keeps walking, lighter now, with a long way still to go.

Name one weight you've carried so long you've stopped noticing it: a grudge, a worry, a regret. Breathe out and let your shoulders drop, as if the straps had loosened on their own. If you pray, bring it to the cross, or rest with come unto me; if you don't, let it be set down for now.
Sepulchre. In Bunyan's dream, the tomb at the foot of the cross where Christian's burden tumbles in and is never seen again.
Your line: the burden rolled away. Lighter, with road still ahead. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians bring their burdens to God in different ways: in personal prayer, in confession or the sacrament of reconciliation, at the communion table, or by laying a written worry at the foot of a cross in some churches.

Evangelist lifts it off his back at the gate and carries it for him.

notes: Check the two Bunyan quotations against a public-domain edition (punctuation and capitalization vary between editions).
Theological framing: the script presents Bunyan's Protestant picture of grace as his, and names other churches' ways (sacraments, confession) without ranking. A Keeper may want different wording.
'Laying a written worry at the foot of a cross in some churches' in howItsDone: a common practice, but confirm the phrasing.

Editor: cut the stock line 'here's the detail worth carrying'; matched the road description more closely to Bunyan (burdened Christian runs, with difficulty, up a highway fenced on either side with a wall).
Second editor pass: Bunyan doesn't say whose sepulchre it is, so 'the place of Christ's own burial' became 'which some readers take as Christ's own tomb'.
